newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate panel approved FDA reform proposal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate panel approved FDA reform proposal.

text.p: A Senate committee on Wednesday easily approved a proposal to revamp the Food and Drug Administration and attempt to further speed up drug approval.

The proposal was less drastic, and therefore less controversial, than a bid to overhaul the FDA in the last Congress. The Senate Labour and Human Resources Committee approved it, 14-4, with four of the panel's eight Democrats joining the Republican majority.
The House of Representatives has not yet taken up related legislation.

"This legislation will give thousands of Americans faster access to new drugs while retaining the FDA's important oversight responsiblities," said committee chairman Sen. James Jeffords, a Vermont Republican.
"There is a risk in approving unsafe drugs, and there is a risk in not approving safe drugs that improve and save thousands of lives. I believe that this bill finds a good balance," he said.
The bill renews the Prescription Drug User Fee Act, under which pharmaceutical companies pay fees that help the FDA meet the cost of speeding up drug approval.
Unless Congress enacts such an extension swiftly, some FDA drug approval staff could face layoff notices late this summer.
The bill would have the agency concentrate its resources on higher risk drugs and devices, and would also allow the FDA to contract with qualified outside examiners to do safety and efficacy reviews.

It would expand humanitarian access to drugs still going through the approval process, and would also make it easier for the FDA to approve a drug for additional purposes, for instance for pediatric use.

Once a drug is approved for one purpose or population group, a doctor can legally prescribe it for another indication but insurance companies do not necessarily reimburse such treatment. Drug companies are sometimes reluctant to go through the costly process of running clinical trials and seeking additional labeling approval for a drug that is already on the market.
